name: Melanotan II
lead: Melanotan II (MT-II) is a synthetic cyclic peptide analogue of the hormone alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH). It stimulates melanin production and was originally developed as a sunless tanning agent; it also increases sexual arousal in some users [1][2]. It acts as a non-selective agonist at several melanocortin receptors, which is why its effects extend beyond skin pigmentation to appetite and erections [1].

Melanotan II has never been approved as a medicine. Development as a sexual-dysfunction drug was dropped in 2000 in favour of a related compound, bremelanotide, which was later approved by the US FDA for low sexual desire in women. Unlicensed melanotan II is nonetheless sold online and informally in some gyms and salons, and health agencies in several countries have issued warnings against its use since 2007 [1]. It is a different compound from afamelanotide (originally called melanotan I), which is an approved prescription drug for a rare light-sensitivity disorder [1].

Small early human trials in the 1990s examined its tanning and erectogenic effects, and later literature consists mostly of case reports and reviews describing adverse events such as priapism, renal infarction, rhabdomyolysis and new or changing moles [3][4][5][6]. Whether it affects melanoma risk is unresolved; reviews note that reported melanomas in users coincided with heavy ultraviolet exposure [1]. It is discussed in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities as a way to obtain a tan with less sun exposure [7][8].

paras: The main appearance use is skin darkening. Users inject the peptide under the skin or use a nasal spray with the aim of building a tan with less ultraviolet exposure, and some also report increased freckling [1][7]. Forum participants in bodybuilding communities describe it as an alternative or complement to spray tans before contests [9][10].

Melanotan II has no approved medical use. It was investigated in the 1990s for psychogenic erectile dysfunction, and that line of work led to bremelanotide, a chemically similar drug later approved for low sexual desire in women [1][11]. A registered phase 2 trial is examining melanotan II as an adjunct to narrowband UVB phototherapy for repigmentation in stable non-segmental vitiligo [12].

A pilot phase I study published in 1996 evaluated melanotan II in human volunteers [13]. A controlled study of its effects on penile erection and sexual motivation was published in 2000 [14]. A double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study in ten men with psychogenic erectile dysfunction found that eight developed clinically apparent erections after melanotan II; mean duration of greater than 80 percent tip rigidity was about 38 minutes versus 3 minutes with placebo. Nausea, stretching, yawning and reduced appetite were reported more often with the drug [11].

Most of the controlled tanning data come from melanotan I (afamelanotide, also called NDP-MSH) rather than melanotan II. Trials reported increased eumelanin and tanning in humans [15], examined its pharmacokinetics by different routes [16], and in 77 Caucasian participants found increased melanin density including in people with MC1R variant genotypes [17].

No randomized trial has tested melanotan II as a cosmetic tanning product against placebo over a sustained period, and no long-term safety data exist. Case reports and reviews describe harms in unregulated users, including low-flow priapism requiring urological intervention [18], renal infarction [19], new or atypical melanocytic naevi [20][21], a melanoma case report [22] and an oral mucosal melanoma case in a nasal-spray user [23]. A systematic review of self-tanning agents also lists rhabdomyolysis, renal infarction and priapism among serious adverse effects of unregulated melanotan I and II use [24].

A review of eruptive melanocytic naevi identified immunosuppressants, chemotherapy or melanotan as the suspected cause in 41 percent of 179 reported patients (grouped together), and five associated melanoma cases across the whole set [21].

Reported effects include nausea, facial flushing, fatigue, stretching, yawning, reduced appetite and spontaneous erections [1][2][11]. Reversible darkening of existing moles and freckles is also described [1].

Case reports describe priapism [18], renal infarction [19] and rhabdomyolysis [24]. Dermatology case literature describes atypical or changing naevi after injection [20] and melanoma in users [22][23].

Causality for melanoma is unresolved. A 2013 review found no conclusive evidence that melanotan II causes melanoma, and a 2021 review concluded that the higher melanoma risk seen in users could probably be explained by greater UV exposure from sun-seeking behaviour; a 2020 animal study reported suppression of melanoma progression [1]. A 2014 dermatology review of tanning noted that the development of alpha-MSH analogues is recent and carries risks alongside the tanning benefit [25]. A 2015 German dermatology review of pigmentation disorders describes melanotan I (as sold online) as dangerous, citing case reports of activated dysplastic naevi [26].
Because products are sold outside regulatory oversight, health agencies warn of uncertain purity, sterility and content [1].

Melanotan II is a non-selective agonist at the melanocortin receptors MC1, MC3, MC4 and MC5. Activation of MC1R on melanocytes drives melanogenesis, while its sexual effects are thought to involve MC4R (with a possible MC3R role); appetite suppression is also attributed to MC4R activation [1]. In rodents, MC4R knockout animals are insensitive to the metabolic-rate and food-intake effects of the compound [27]. It is partly metabolised to bremelanotide [1].

Melanotan II is a lactam-bridged cyclic heptapeptide, written Ac-Nle-cyclo[Asp-His-D-Phe-Arg-Trp-Lys]-NH2, with a molecular formula of C50H69N15O9 [2]. Relative to native alpha-MSH, it substitutes norleucine for methionine and D-phenylalanine for L-phenylalanine, changes associated with greater stability and potency [2]. A published synthesis route proceeds in 12 steps with a reported overall yield of 2.6 percent [1].

Research in the early 1960s found that alpha-MSH caused sexual arousal in rats. In the 1980s, scientists at the University of Arizona began developing alpha-MSH analogues as sunless tanning agents and synthesised melanotan I and melanotan II. One researcher who self-experimented with an early melanotan II tool compound reportedly injected twice the intended dose and had an eight-hour erection with nausea and vomiting [1]. The pharmacology of both analogues was reviewed in 1998 [28].

Melanotan I was licensed through a technology-transfer company to an Australian start-up, Epitan, renamed Clinuvel in 2006; it became afamelanotide, approved by the FDA in 2019. Melanotan II was licensed to Palatin Technologies, which stopped developing it in 2000 and pursued bremelanotide instead. A contract dispute was settled in 2008, with rights to melanotan II returning to the technology-transfer company and Palatin paying US$800,000 [1].

Melanotan II is not approved by the FDA or the European Medicines Agency for any use, and sellers' products are described as unapproved and not legal for human use in any jurisdiction. Health agencies in various countries, including the UK and Australia, have warned against its use since 2007 [1][2].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness communities
paras: Guides and walkthroughs on looksmax.org discuss melanotan-1 and melanotan-2 as tanning peptides [29][30][31]. On T Nation, threads from 2008 onward include informational stickies, first-cycle questions and remarks that physique competitors may be using it for very dark skin [9][10][32][33]. Some posters also mention its erectogenic effect, including one 2023 post describing an erection after a dose and comparing it with PT-141 [34].

Current work includes the registered vitiligo phototherapy adjunct trial [12]. Recent 2026 publications include a case report on social-media misinformation about melanotan II, a case of tachycardia and rhabdomyolysis after melanotan use, and systematic reviews of peptides for male sexual dysfunction [35][36][37]. A broader review discusses benefits and risks of chronic MC1R activation [38].

lore.intro: In bodybuilding and looksmaxxing forums, melanotan II is discussed as a way to darken skin with less sun exposure, with threads sharing protocols and experiences and occasionally mentioning libido effects [9][29][34].

claims.claim: It produces a deep, lasting tan with minimal UV exposure
claims.believers: Forum members describe holding a tan for a long time without deliberately sunbathing and suggest it allows a tan with less UV exposure than tanning beds [9][32].
claims.experts: Controlled trials of the closely related melanotan I showed increased eumelanin and tanning in humans [15][17]. No placebo-controlled trial of unlicensed melanotan II as a tanning product has been published [13].

claims.claim: It is a safe way to protect skin from sunburn
claims.believers: Posters on T Nation have described it as a way to obtain a safe tan while minimising ageing UV exposure [33].
claims.experts: Dermatology reviews describe case reports of atypical naevi and melanoma in users, with causality unresolved and confounded by UV exposure [1][20][22][25].

claims.claim: It boosts libido and causes spontaneous erections
claims.believers: Users report strong erections after dosing, and one poster discussed it alongside PT-141 for erectile problems [34].
claims.experts: A double-blind crossover study found erections in 8 of 10 men with psychogenic erectile dysfunction [11]. Priapism has been reported in an unregulated user [18].

claims.claim: Gray-market melanotan is the same as prescription afamelanotide
claims.believers: Community guides group melanotan 1 and 2 together as tanning peptides [31].
claims.experts: Afamelanotide is a licensed prescription drug for a specific rare condition, while melanotan II is unapproved and a distinct molecule [1].

claims.claim: Melanotan has been used by physique competitors for very dark skin
claims.believers: T Nation posters remark that competitors looked unnaturally dark and attribute it to melanotan or fake tan [10][39].
claims.experts: No published studies document prevalence among competitors; reviews describe unregulated use and adverse events generally [24].

claims.claim: Unregulated melanotan carries risks to kidneys, moles and other organs
claims.believers: Proponents in forum guides present melanotan use as manageable with preparation and discuss side effects as part of their walkthroughs [29][31].
claims.experts: Case reports document renal infarction, rhabdomyolysis, new moles and melanoma in users, and agencies warn about purity and sterility [1][19][24].
